{"data":{"id":"ghr65_v1","type":"preprints","attributes":{"date_created":"2026-11-14T07:50:56.479028","date_modified":"2026-11-14T20:45:13.916478","date_published":"2026-11-14T20:45:13.889877","original_publication_date":null,"custom_publication_citation":null,"doi":null,"title":"The wealth of algorithms: generative AI, jobs and inequality in a global dynamic CGE model","description":"This paper models how generative artificial intelligence (AI) affects jobs, wages and inequality across the
world economy. Few doubt that it will change the economy; what nobody yet knows is how. Workers, firms
and governments want to know whose jobs and pay will change, who will capture the gains and which
countries will come out ahead, well before the evidence can tell them. This paper does not try to forecast that
future. Its contribution is a quantitative framework for understanding what drives AI’s economic effects, what
they depend on, and what follows for policy. We add AI to a global dynamic computable general equilibrium
(CGE) model that tracks production, trade, investment and employment year by year to 2040 in 23 regions. AI
does some tasks inside each occupation and makes workers more productive in others. When AI does a task, we
start from a 27% saving on its labour cost, the average Acemoglu (2025) draws from two workplace
experiments. We run a central scenario and 68 alternatives that vary how fast and how widely AI is adopted,
what it costs, how far it replaces rather than helps workers and how labour markets adjust.

How cheap and capable AI becomes, and how widely firms adopt it, decide the size of the gain: by 2040 world
GDP ends about 1% to 15% above a path without AI in our main scenarios (about 7% in the central case). It
reaches about 35% in an extreme case where AI becomes 30% a year more efficient (15 to 25% if AI keeps
improving but more slowly over time). Most of the gain goes to owners of capital in almost every scenario.
Who shares in it depends on who owns capital and on the extent to which AI replaces rather than helps
workers. In the central case capital’s share of world income rises by about 4 points, clerks’ real pay ends
roughly 13 to 22% below the no-AI path in the large economies, and within rich economies the Gini coefficient
of household income rises by about 2 to 3.5 points. If job losses last, the world gain against the no-AI baseline
in 2040 is 5.4% against 6.8%, and labour income falls further everywhere.

Based on these results, we then test several illustrative AI policies to see how they change the outcomes and
their distributional effects. Each does a different job: support for changing jobs mainly protects workers’ pay,
keeping AI cheap mainly protects output, and only sharing AI’s capital income narrows inequality noticeably.
The policies are illustrative and largely unfunded in the model, so their gains are likely
